title: FDA Approves First RAS-Targeted Drug for Pancreatic Cancer After Trial Nearly Doubles Survival
excerpt: Daraxonrasib, sold as Rasonque, is a once-daily pill that extended median survival to 13.2 months from 6.7 months on chemotherapy in a phase 3 trial of 500 patients.
body:
• The FDA has approved daraxonrasib (brand name Rasonque), the first oral RAS inhibitor for metastatic pancreatic cancer, a disease with a five-year survival rate of just 3% at stage IV.
  • In a phase 3 trial of 500 patients, daraxonrasib nearly doubled median overall survival to 13.2 months compared with 6.7 months on standard chemotherapy.
  • The once-daily pill targets KRAS mutations that drive more than 90% of the most common form of pancreatic cancer — a protein family researchers spent over 40 years trying to drug.
  • The approval does not replace chemotherapy as first-line treatment but gives patients a targeted alternative after their cancer progresses on initial therapy.

Cracking an Undruggable Target

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration on Tuesday approved daraxonrasib, a once-daily pill that nearly doubles survival for patients with metastatic pancreatic cancer, ending a four-decade quest to develop a drug against one of oncology's most elusive targets.

Sold under the brand name Rasonque, the drug is the first approved therapy to block multiple forms of the RAS protein family — a group of molecules involved in cell growth that have been central to cancer biology since mutations were first identified in human tumors in the early 1980s. KRAS mutations drive more than 90% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, the most common form of the disease.

"The FDA approval of daraxonrasib represents a landmark advance for patients with metastatic pancreatic cancer. The nearly doubling of median overall survival time seen with this targeted treatment represents meaningful progress for patients where new treatment options are urgently needed."

— Brian Wolpin, MD, Director of the Hale Family Center for Pancreatic Cancer Research, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute

The Trial That Changed the Standard

The approval was based on the pivotal RASolute 302 trial, an international, randomized phase 3 study led by Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. The trial enrolled 500 adults with previously treated metastatic pancreatic cancer and compared daraxonrasib as a single agent against another course of chemotherapy.

Patients taking daraxonrasib lived a median of 13.2 months, compared with 6.7 months for those receiving chemotherapy. Median progression-free survival — the period before the cancer worsened — was 7.2 months versus 3.6 months. Patients on the drug also experienced significantly longer periods before their pain worsened and their quality of life deteriorated, according to results published in the New England Journal of Medicine.

"There's no doubt that this is the best available treatment for patients who've had previous chemo," said Peter Hosein, a medical oncologist at Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center, which participated in the trial.

Why This Drug Is Different

Earlier KRAS-targeted drugs, such as sotorasib approved in 2021 for lung cancer, zeroed in on a single mutation called KRAS G12C — relatively uncommon in pancreatic cancer. Daraxonrasib takes a broader approach. It is "multiselective," designed to block the active forms of several RAS proteins and mutations. The FDA indication does not require patients to have a particular mutation to receive it.

That breadth sets Rasonque apart from existing targeted treatments for pancreatic cancer, which apply only to small groups of patients with uncommon genetic features. BRCA-targeted therapies, for example, apply to roughly 5% to 8% of patients, while some other options are relevant to fewer than 1%.

The drug also offers a practical advantage: it is an oral pill, sparing patients the burden of IV infusions or portable chemotherapy pumps. Side effects graded severe or worse occurred in 61.8% of daraxonrasib patients versus 69.6% on chemotherapy, and only 1.2% of patients discontinued treatment due to side effects, compared with 11.2% on chemotherapy.

Limits and What's Ahead

Rasonque is approved for adults whose metastatic pancreatic cancer has already been treated with at least one systemic therapy, or who are not candidates for multi-drug treatment. It does not replace chemotherapy as first-line treatment for most patients.

An ongoing phase 3 trial is evaluating daraxonrasib alone and in combination with chemotherapy for previously untreated metastatic disease. Researchers are also investigating whether the drug can prevent recurrence after surgery.

"I don't think that the news can be overstated. It's nothing short of a paradigm-shifting, historical approval."

— Peter Hosein, Medical Oncologist, Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center

The drug is not a cure. Patients who respond well can eventually develop resistance, and researchers do not yet understand why some remain on the drug far longer than others. More than 70 additional KRAS inhibitors for pancreatic cancer are currently in development.

Pancreatic cancer remains one of the deadliest forms of the disease. There is no routine screening for the general population, few early warning signs, and the cancer tends to spread quickly. Most patients are first diagnosed at stage IV, where the five-year survival rate is just 3%. The FDA approved Rasonque several months ahead of its expected decision deadline.
nri_angle: The approval opens a new treatment option for pancreatic cancer patients worldwide, including in the Indian-American community where gastrointestinal cancers carry significant health burden.
